questions.question: What is inheritance in Java and how do you implement it?
questions.title: Inheritance in Java with extends Keyword
questions.direct_answer: **Inheritance** is the OOP mechanism where a subclass acquires the non-private fields and methods of a superclass using the `extends` keyword. It models an **IS-A relationship** — a `Dog` IS-A `Animal`. The subclass can reuse, extend, or override the parent's behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of the extends keyword, IS-A relationship, and what is actually inherited
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying private members are inherited — they are not accessible in the subclass (though they exist in the object)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify that private members are part of the object in memory but not accessible — protected members ARE accessible in subclasses

sections.title: extends — Building on Existing Classes
Key Points
sections.content:
- `extends` keyword establishes inheritance
- IS-A relationship: `Dog extends Animal` means every Dog IS-A Animal
- Subclass inherits all `public` and `protected` fields and methods
- `private` members of the parent are NOT accessible in the subclass
- Java supports only **single class inheritance** (one parent class)
- A class implicitly extends `Object` if no `extends` clause is specified
- The subclass can add new fields/methods and override inherited methods

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Inheritance in Java is implemented using the `extends` keyword. It models an IS-A relationship — so a `Dog extends Animal` means every Dog is an Animal and gets all of Animal's public and protected members. The subclass can use those inherited methods as-is, add new methods, or override existing ones. One important point: private members of the parent class are not accessible in the subclass, even though they technically exist in the object's memory. Java only supports single inheritance for classes to avoid the diamond problem.

questions.question: Why does Java not support multiple inheritance for classes?
questions.title: Why Java Doesn't Support Multiple Inheritance
questions.direct_answer: Java avoids multiple class inheritance to prevent the **diamond problem** — the ambiguity that arises when two parent classes define the same method and the compiler can't determine which one to inherit. Java solves this by allowing a class to implement **multiple interfaces** instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the diamond problem and Java's design decision to use interfaces for multiple inheritance of type
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Java doesn't support any form of multiple inheritance — it does through interfaces
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java 8 introduced default methods in interfaces, and Java resolves the diamond conflict by requiring the implementing class to override the ambiguous method

sections.title: The Diamond Problem
sections.content:
Imagine this scenario (not valid Java, but hypothetical):

```
       A.display()
      /         \
   B.display()   C.display()
      \         /
         D  ???
```

If `D` extends both `B` and `C`, and both override `A.display()` differently, which `display()` does `D` inherit? This ambiguity is the **diamond problem**.

Java's solution: **classes can only extend one class**, but can **implement multiple interfaces**.

```java
interface Flyable { void fly(); }
interface Swimmable { void swim(); }

class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable { // multiple interfaces: OK!
    public void fly() { System.out.println("Flying"); }
    public void swim() { System.out.println("Swimming"); }
}
```

With Java 8 default methods, a version of the diamond problem can occur in interfaces too — but Java resolves it by **requiring the implementing class to explicitly override** the conflicting method.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Diamond problem: ambiguity when two parents have the same method with different implementations
- Java prevents this by restricting classes to single inheritance
- Java supports **multiple interface implementation** — a class can `implement` multiple interfaces
- Java 8 default methods in interfaces can cause a similar issue — resolved by mandatory override in the implementing class
- C++ supports multiple inheritance but uses complex resolution rules
- Composition (HAS-A) is often preferred over inheritance (IS-A) to avoid tight coupling

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Java doesn't support multiple class inheritance to avoid the diamond problem. Imagine class D inheriting from both B and C, which both override the same method from A. The compiler wouldn't know which version to use in D — that's the ambiguity. Java's solution is to restrict classes to a single parent but allow implementing multiple interfaces, since interfaces (before Java 8) had no implementation to conflict. With Java 8 default methods, the conflict can still arise with interfaces, but Java resolves it by requiring the implementing class to override the conflicting method explicitly.

questions.question: How does constructor chaining work with super() in inheritance?
questions.title: Constructor Chaining with super() in Java
questions.direct_answer: When a subclass object is created, the **parent class constructor must run first**. If you don't explicitly call `super()` in the subclass constructor, Java implicitly inserts `super()` (no-arg). If the parent has no no-arg constructor, you must explicitly call the appropriate `super(...)` as the **first statement**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the implicit super() call, the first-statement rule, and what happens when the parent has no no-arg constructor
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Java implicitly inserts super() — or not knowing that a compile error occurs when the parent has only parameterized constructors
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that this ensures the parent part of the object is always fully initialized before the child's constructor runs

sections.title: Parent Constructor Always Runs First
Key Points
sections.content:
- Java implicitly inserts `super()` if you don't write any super() call
- `super()` must be the first statement in a constructor
- If the parent has no no-arg constructor, you MUST explicitly call the right `super(args...)` 
- Parent constructor always runs before child constructor body
- This ensures the full parent part of the object is initialized first
- You cannot have both `this()` and `super()` in the same constructor
- The chain goes all the way up to `Object` — every object construction ends with `Object()`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When you create a subclass object, the parent's constructor always runs first. If you don't explicitly call `super()` in the subclass constructor, Java inserts it automatically — but that only works if the parent has a no-arg constructor. If the parent only has parameterized constructors, you must explicitly call `super(arguments)` as the very first statement in your constructor, or you'll get a compile error. This guarantees that the parent portion of the object is fully initialized before the child's constructor body runs.

followup_questions: What compile error do you get when you forget to call super() for a parent with only parameterized constructors?

questions.question: What is the difference between method overriding and method hiding in Java?
questions.title: Method Overriding vs Method Hiding in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Method overriding** applies to instance methods — the subclass version is called based on the **actual object type at runtime** (dynamic dispatch). **Method hiding** applies to `static` methods — the subclass defines a static method with the same signature, but which version runs is determined by the **reference type at compile time**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that static methods are not polymorphic — static dispatch vs dynamic dispatch
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying static methods can be overridden — they can only be hidden, and virtual dispatch does not apply
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the code example where the reference type determines which static method runs, even if the object is of the subclass type

sections.title: Static vs Instance — Two Different Dispatch Mechanisms
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Overriding**: instance methods, resolved at **runtime** based on actual object type
- **Hiding**: static methods, resolved at **compile time** based on reference type
- Use `@Override` annotation for instance method overriding (compile-time check)
- `@Override` on a static method causes a compile error — can't override static
- Static methods are associated with the class, not with object instances
- Method hiding is considered bad practice — prefer not redefining static methods in subclasses
- Both require the same method signature (name + parameters)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Method overriding applies to instance methods and is resolved at runtime based on the actual object type — this is how polymorphism works. Method hiding applies to static methods — if a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as the parent's static method, it hides it. The key difference is: for instance methods, even if the reference type is the parent, the child's method is called because the JVM checks the actual object. For static methods, the reference type determines which version runs, because static methods are bound at compile time.

questions.question: How do you use super to access parent class members in Java?
questions.title: Using super to Access Parent Members in Java
questions.direct_answer: `super` is a reference to the parent class. Use `super.field` to access a hidden parent field, `super.method()` to call an overridden parent method, and `super()` in a constructor to call the parent's constructor. `super` cannot be used in static contexts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of the three uses of super and when each is needed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using super.method() unnecessarily when there's no override, or trying to use super in a static method
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the practical use case: calling super.method() to extend parent behavior rather than completely replace it

sections.title: Three Ways to Use super
Key Points
sections.content:
- `super()` — calls parent constructor; must be the first statement
- `super.method()` — calls the parent's version of an overridden method
- `super.field` — accesses a parent field hidden by a child field with the same name
- `super` cannot be used in `static` methods (no object context)
- Unlike `this`, `super` cannot be assigned or passed as a parameter
- Common pattern: override method calls `super.method()` then adds extra behavior
- Chaining: `super` refers to the direct parent, not grandparent or beyond (from within a method)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The `super` keyword has three uses. First, `super()` in a constructor calls the parent's constructor. Second, `super.method()` inside an overriding method calls the parent's version — this is useful when you want to extend the parent's behavior rather than replace it entirely. Third, `super.field` accesses a parent field that's been hidden by a child field with the same name. You cannot use `super` in a static method because there's no object context. The most practical use I encounter is calling `super.method()` to add to rather than replace parent behavior.

followup_questions: Can you chain super calls to reach a grandparent class?

questions.question: What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A relationships in Java?
questions.title: IS-A vs HAS-A Relationship in Java
questions.direct_answer: **IS-A** (inheritance) means one class is a subtype of another — `Dog` IS-A `Animal`, implemented with `extends`. **HAS-A** (composition) means one class contains a reference to another as a field — `Car` HAS-A `Engine`, implemented by having an `Engine` field in `Car`. Composition is often preferred over inheritance for flexibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding when to use inheritance vs composition, a fundamental design decision
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using inheritance when composition would be more appropriate, creating fragile hierarchies
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'favor composition over inheritance' principle from the Gang of Four, and explain why — composition is more flexible and avoids tight coupling

sections.title: Inheritance vs Composition
Key Points
sections.content:
- IS-A: inheritance (`extends`), subtype relationship, `Dog instanceof Animal` is true
- HAS-A: composition (field reference), reuse through containment
- Ask: 'Is X truly a Y?' — if unsure, prefer HAS-A
- Composition allows behavior to be changed at runtime (swap the component)
- Inheritance creates tight coupling — changes to parent can break subclasses
- Composition favors interfaces — `Car` has an `Engine` interface, can swap implementations
- 'Favor composition over inheritance' — Gang of Four Design Patterns

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: IS-A is inheritance — `Dog extends Animal` because a Dog is genuinely a type of Animal. HAS-A is composition — `Car` has an `Engine` because a Car contains an Engine but isn't a type of Engine. The design principle is to favor composition over inheritance when possible. Composition is more flexible — you can swap implementations at runtime, there's less coupling, and changes to one component don't cascade through a hierarchy. I'd use inheritance when the IS-A relationship is clear, stable, and the subclass truly represents a specialization of the parent.

followup_questions: Why do design patterns favor composition over inheritance?
Can you give an example where using inheritance was the wrong choice?
How does dependency injection relate to the HAS-A relationship?
